newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. extradition ruling hits raw nerve in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: U.S. extradition ruling hits raw nerve in Hong Kong.

text.p: When a U.S. judge ruled this week against extraditing a fugitive to Hong Kong because of the 1997 handover to China, he struck a very raw nerve.

"If this is the level of understanding in the United States of Hong Kong after the handover, then we have a major task ahead of us educating those who should know better," the Hong Kong Standard said in an editorial on Thursday.

Hong Kong people harbour many concerns about the future yet few seriously expect to see judges de-wigged and replaced by magistrates dispensing summary justice in show-trials from the benches of the high court.

But this was the prospect painted by Boston District Court Judge Joseph Tauro on Tuesday when he refused to return a suspect facing bribery and conspiracy charges to Hong Kong for trial, the South China Morning Post said on Thursday.
"It is, to say the least, unhelpful if those who presume to pass judgement on us believe that the territory will turn into a place where summary justice is handed out in show trials," the Post said.

If there is one belief that Hong Kong people cling to in the countdown to the handover at midnight on June 30, 1997, it is that Beijing will largely honour its pledge that Hong Kong will continue to enjoy freedoms unheard of on the mainland.
Defendent Jerry Lui Kin-hong argued he may face execution because Hong Kong would be a part of China after the handover.
The decision, the Post said, "flies in the face of the fact that the territory will continue to enjoy the common law, administered by an independent judiciary, after the handover."
Capital punishment has been abolished in Hong Kong where no executions have been carried out since 1966.
Executions are widespread in China.
The South China Morning Post seized on the irony of the ruling coinciding with an announcement of a triple execution in the state of Arkansas.
The 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration governing the handover binds China to permitting Hong Kong's six million people to maintaining their freewheeling capitalist way of life intact for 50 years.
Hong Kong's social, political and, importantly, its legal system based on English common law, would continue to prevail.

"If foreign courts doubt or disbelieve this, then Hong Kong needs to do more to tell people what it will be like after June 30," said Nellie Fong, executive director of the Better Hong Kong Foundation, a pro-Beijing business lobby.

The Boston court's decision irked Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten who has sprearheaded an ambitious government campaign to spread the word internationally about Hong Kong's status under China's one country, two systems policy.
"That's embodied in an international treaty. And we don't think it should be questioned by anyone."
He said Hong Kong would mount an immediate appeal against the ruling.
But Hong Kong's pro-democracy activists say they fear that China will ride roughshod over promised freedoms and it was not surprising that the American judge reached his conclusion.

"We're already seeing from their (China's) actions Hong Kong will not have a high degree of autonomy," said pro-democracy activist Emily Lau, pointing to Beijing's decision to scuttle Hong Kong's elected legislature.

China will replace the 60-member body with an appointed provisional chamber, made up of staunchly pro-Beijing deputies including several defeated in Hong Kong's last election, rolling back at a stroke recent democratic reforms.
